findings.headline: Planned savings of £36m are at risk: £0.375m shortfall forecast at Q1, with ongoing delivery risks in Legal Services and Business Support
findings.detail: Revenue budget approved by Full Council included efficiency savings of £36m. Budget Summit savings target £15.1m but forecast to deliver only £14.8m (£0.3m shortfall), largely in Adult Care and Community Wellbeing where savings remain dependent on service redesign, system changes, and workforce optimisation. Other MTFP savings target £21.5m and forecast to deliver £21.4m (£0.1m shortfall) in Resources on property rationalisation. Total shortfall £0.375m. Report flags 'risks remain within Business Support and Legal Services.' Legal Services affected by continued reliance on locums, recruitment difficulties, and uncertainty over income (£0.380m pressure).
findings.matters: Savings slippage reduces usable headroom and signals assumed productivity improvements or asset sales may not land. At quarter 1, forecasted savings already 1% adrift. With 9 months to go and delivery risks flagged, larger slippage is possible. A lender needs to know whether 2027/28 budget can be balanced without relying on similar risky savings.
findings.figures: Planned savings £36m; forecast delivery £35.625m (shortfall £0.375m or 1%); Budget Summit £15.1m planned vs £14.8m forecast; MTFP savings £21.5m planned vs £21.4m forecast; Legal Services pressure £0.380m
findings.quote: At quarter one, Budget Summit savings of £14.8m are forecast against a planned £15.1m, resulting in a £0.3m shortfall... Unachieved savings are being monitored through monthly budget holder meetings, with alternative plans required where original proposals are delayed or no longer deliverable.

findings.headline: LOBO loan of £10m with BAE Systems can be called by lender on 31 December 2026; if called, council will repay
findings.detail: Long-term debt includes LOBO loan of £10m from BAE Systems at 4%, maturing 31 December 2061. First call period falls on 31 December 2026. If lender calls the option, council will reject the lender's option to extend and will repay £10m. Fixed debt maturing in 2026/27 is £6.304m. Next call period on LOBO loans will be 31 December 2031. This possibility has been factored into cash flow for the year.
findings.matters: LOBO call removes certainty about liquidity. If BAE Systems calls option and council repays £10m, it adds to cash outflow during Q4 2026/27. Given forecast need for £33.5m external borrowing if reserves drawn, £10m LOBO repayment in December 2026 would tighten year-end liquidity.
findings.figures: LOBO loan £10m at 4% with BAE Systems; call date 31 December 2026; repayment required if called; next call dates 31 December 2031 (then every 5 years); fixed debt maturing 2026/27 £6.304m
findings.quote: Debt maturing in the year is £6.304m, however there is a possibility that an existing LOBO loan of £10m from BAE Systems may be called on 31 December 2026 and if so, this will be repaid.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing requirement increased from £82.6m to £133.4m due to carry-forward from prior year; external borrowing of £33.5m may still be needed if reserves are drawn
findings.detail: Long-term borrowing requirement for 2026/27 updated for carry-forward from 2025/26, additions and rephasing, bringing new requirement to £133.4m from original £82.6m. Capital programme underspend of £56.5m forecast to reduce to £76.98m. At this level, Debt Liability Benchmark suggests no external borrowing required to maintain £50m liquidity threshold. However, if predicted reserve use materialises, council would need to borrow approximately £33.5m in 2026/27 to maintain £50m liquidity threshold. External borrowing not to be taken until March 2027.
findings.matters: Borrowing requirement has grown significantly. Contingency on whether external borrowing needed (£33.5m) depends on reserve use actually happening—which is likely given demand pressures. A lender needs to assess headline capital financing looks manageable only if reserves do not deteriorate further.
findings.figures: Capital borrowing requirement £82.6m (budget) → £133.4m (carry-forward + additions) → £76.98m (after programme underspend); conditional external borrowing £33.5m if reserves drawn; existing long-term debt £437.18m at 3.67%; total debt if £33.5m borrowed: £470.01m at 3.75%; Capital Financing Charges 3.57% of income (vs 10% voluntary limit)
findings.quote: Long-term borrowing requirement for 2026/27 has been updated for carry forward from 2025/26, additions and rephasing of the capital programme in the quarter leaving the new requirement at £133.4m, from £82.6m... However, if predicted use of reserves takes place, as outlined in Appendix C, then this would mean that around £33.5m of external borrowing would be required to maintain the £50m liquidity threshold.

findings.headline: Total reserves forecast to fall from £137.5m to £58.4m during 2026/27, with school reserves moving into deficit
findings.detail: At 31 March 2026, total reserves stood at £137.5m. During 2026/27, forecast to reduce to £58.4m. Most significant movement in School Reserves (£43m), comprising school balances and DSG Adjustment Account holding 2025/26 deficit (£25m) and forecast 2026/27 deficit (£52m), offset by anticipated High Needs Stability Grant support for 90% of 2025/26 deficit. General Fund reserves expected to hold at £48.1m. Report notes 'forecast use of reserves provides some short-term financial resilience but does not address underlying causes of cost pressures.'
findings.matters: A reserve of £58.4m on £870m budget is just 6.7%. School reserve is in deficit and statutory. General fund reserve of £48.1m includes £24.2m General Fund (2.8% of budget) and £24m Financial Volatility Reserve (2.8%). Usable reserves limited. If demand pressures worsen or other risks materialize, council has limited headroom and would need to borrow or reduce spending.
findings.figures: Total reserves £137.5m (March 2026) → £58.4m (forecast March 2027), fall of 57%; School reserves move £43m; DSG deficit grows £25m → £54.3m; General Fund reserves £24.2m; Financial Volatility Reserve £24m
findings.quote: The total reserves balance on 31 March 2026 was £137.5m. During 2026/27, this is forecast to reduce to £58.4m... the forecast use of reserves provides some short-term financial resilience but does not address the underlying causes of cost pressures from ongoing demand and inflationary increases.

findings.headline: Core contingency budget nearly exhausted: £5.348m of £6.0m committed, leaving only £0.652m buffer plus £1.5m TROs income contingency
findings.detail: Council holds £7.5m total contingency (£6.0m core plus £1.5m TROs income offset). £5.348m committed: £2.938m for high-cost secure placements, £1.128m for SEND workforce, £0.367m for IT invest-to-save, £0.315m for emPSN exit, £0.300m Tour of Britain, £0.300m Harrowby United 3G pitch. Leaves £0.652m core contingency unallocated. TROs contingency (£1.5m) is for unachieved income and expected not to be needed in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Contingency is buffer against forecast errors and unexpected events. With Q1 already showing variances and 9 months remaining, £0.652m buffer on £799.8m budget is very tight (0.08%). Council acknowledged risks in demand-led budgets and forecast volatility. Minimal headroom if assumptions deteriorate.
findings.figures: £6.0m core contingency with £5.348m committed (89% spent); £0.652m remaining; £1.5m TROs contingency; £799.8m net revenue budget
findings.quote: Of the £6.0m core contingency, commitments totalling £5.348m are forecast... The remaining £0.7m of core contingency, together with the uncommitted TRO income contingency of £1.5m, remains unallocated at quarter one.

findings.headline: Underlying demand growth exceeds funding growth; Council explicitly states pressure is recurrent, not one-off, requiring 2027/28 budget action
findings.detail: Report explicitly states £12.6m service overspends are driven by 'pressures within demand-led budgets' and notes: 'Demand for Council services, and particularly complex demand, continues to increase at a faster rate than the Council's funding can increase.' Council acknowledges Q1 forecast shows 'Quarter two monitoring will therefore focus on identifying further mitigating actions and assessing the extent to which recurring pressures will need to be addressed through the 2027/28 budget setting process.' Not treated as timing issue but as structural mismatch.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether deficits are recurrent or one-off. This council is signalling that demand pressures are structural and will need to be absorbed through next budget cycle. This implies either further savings, tax rises, or reserve drawdown in 2027/28.
findings.figures: £12.6m service overspends vs £7.5m contingency + other budget offsets; children's placements £11.7m pressure; transport £3.7m
findings.quote: Demand for Council services, and particularly complex demand, continues to increase at a faster rate than the Council's funding can increase. This gives rise to ongoing challenges which will need to be managed and will be a key area of focus during quarter two and as part of the budget setting exercise for 2027/28.

findings.headline: Home to School Transport overspending by £3.7m and will worsen: SEND demand growth, 6.8% transport CPI inflation, and Government has not funded the shortfall
findings.detail: Place directorate forecasting £3.7m overspend on Home to School Transport. Number of children with EHCPs continuing to increase, cost increases driven by SEND-related demand (68 additional secondary placements during Q1, Day Special transport up £0.040m alone). ONS reported transport prices rose 6.8% in 12 months to May 2026, an increase of 3% from budget-setting time. Number of supplier contract uplift requests in Q1 already matches total received in whole of previous year. Government has not allocated funding through High Needs Stability Grant to support Home to School Transport costs.
findings.matters: This is an unfunded, recurring demand pressure. SEND growth is forecast and inevitable. Transport inflation is exogenous but large. The budget cannot be controlled without reducing SEND provision (which would breach statutory duties). A lender needs to understand this is a permanent structural gap.
findings.figures: £3.684m Q1 overspend on Home to School Transport; 6.8% transport CPI inflation in 12 months to May 2026; weekly cost increase from contract re-procurements £0.077m; EHCPs increasing; no Government High Needs funding allocated to transport
findings.quote: The Place Directorate is forecasting an overspend at quarter one, largely driven by Home to School Transport overspend of £3.684m, with the service continuing to face significant financial pressure, partly driven by sustained growth and demand for SEND places... It is worth noting that the Government has not allocated any funding through the High Needs Stability Grant to support Home to School Transport costs.

findings.headline: Schools DSG deficit forecast to grow from £25m to £54.3m in a single year, with Government funding for only 90% of pre-March 2026 element
findings.detail: High Needs Block forecasting £51.96m overspend at Q1, including a planned £34.5m overspend identified during budget setting. EHCPs forecast to increase from 3,785 to 4,460, adding £8.6m pressure on mainstream top-up funding. Specialist placements at 678 vs budget assumption of 600. DSG reserve deficit expected to move from £25m end-2025/26 to £54.3m end-2026/27. Government indicated it will support approximately 90% of DSG deficits incurred up to 31 March 2026 through grant funding, with proportionate approach for deficits after that date.
findings.matters: Represents a structural financial problem for the council. Even with Government support for 90% of pre-March 2026 element, the council carries a growing deficit. The reserve is ringfenced and statutory rules prevent using general fund reserves to cover it, but it signals unsustainable SEND provision costs.
findings.figures: £25m deficit March 2026 → £54.3m deficit March 2027; £51.96m High Needs Block overspend; EHCPs: 3,785 → 4,460 (add 675); Specialist placements 678 vs budget 600; 90% Government support for pre-31 March 2026 element only
findings.quote: the forecast DSG reserve position is expected to move from a £25m deficit in March 2026 to a £54.3m deficit in March 2027, reflecting the current year overspend after allowing for anticipated High Needs Stability Grant support in respect of the 2025/26 deficit.

findings.headline: Children's independent placements overspending by £11.7m, significantly exceeding budget assumptions set in February
findings.detail: Children's Social Care is forecasting a £9.4m overspend at Q1, driven by independent placements for children in care. Detailed placement analysis shows a £11.7m cost pressure, reflecting both full-year costs of current demand and continued growth in placement numbers during remainder of 2026/27. The scale and speed of growth since October 2025 significantly exceeded assumptions built into the budget. Although FOCUS Fostering Scheme and Reunification Team delivered £5.0m of placement cost reductions exceeding the £4.7m target, this is now substantially outweighed by demand growth.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this is one-off or recurrent. Placement demand is volatile, growing faster than the service can manage, and the budget was already substantially increased in 2026/27. If £11.7m pressure recurs next year, it signals an unfundable demand trajectory.
findings.figures: £11.7m placement cost pressure vs budget; £5.0m transformation savings achieved but overwhelmed; 58.7 per 10,000 children in care (vs 67 for statistical neighbours, 70 nationally); 93 out-of-county placements July 2026 vs 68 in October 2025
findings.quote: independent placements for Children in Care. Detailed placement analysis indicates a total independent placement cost pressure of approximately £11.7m compared with the assumptions built into the 2026/27 budget.

findings.headline: Council explicitly acknowledges 'underlying demand and cost pressures remain a key risk for 2026/27 and beyond'
findings.detail: Despite a £0.499m underspend in 2025/26, the council's own assessment is that underlying demand and cost pressures in social care services remain a key risk for future years. The council has built cost pressures into the 2026/27 budget but acknowledges 'risk from potentially higher demand increases than forecast'. This will be a key focus for Executive monitoring during 2026/27.
findings.matters: The council's risk assessment acknowledges it cannot reliably forecast demand-led cost growth in social care, suggesting future budget challenges are probable and may require difficult service decisions or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £0.499m underspend masks underlying structural pressures
findings.quote: While the outturn is positive, the underlying demand and cost pressures, remain a key risk for 2026/27 and beyond. These pressures were reflected in the 2026/27 budget; however, there remains risk from potentially higher demand increases than forecast.

findings.headline: Capital programme underspent by £50.201m (20%), primarily due to major project delays
findings.detail: The council invested £194.764m in capital during 2025/26, which was £50.201m lower than the planned £244.4m budget. The majority of underspend was due to timing of large-scale projects, particularly major infrastructure schemes such as Grantham Southern Relief Road and North Hykeham Relief Road. A full review of the capital programme is underway to reprofil timelines and costs.
findings.matters: Capital project delays can lead to construction cost inflation (typically 5-15% annually) and may signal delivery risks or resource constraints that could affect the council's ability to deliver planned infrastructure investment.
findings.figures: £50.201m underspend (20% of planned £244.4m); £194.764m actual capital investment
findings.quote: Overall, spending was £50.201 million lower than planned at year end, mainly due to changes in the timing of projects, with spend now expected to take place in future years.

findings.headline: Adult social care overspent by £5.450m despite achieving £4.7m planned savings due to demand growth
findings.detail: Adult social care experienced sustained demand growth that exceeded budget assumptions. During the year, 126 additional people entered direct payment arrangements and 7,158 additional hours of extra care were delivered. Community Supported Living client numbers doubled. Despite achieving approximately £4.7m planned savings plus an additional £1m through transformation, demand pressures overwhelmed these savings.
findings.matters: Demand growth outpacing savings delivery in a statutory service with ageing demographics signals structural affordability challenges that savings programmes cannot offset.
findings.figures: £5.450m overspend; 126 additional direct payment clients; 7,158 additional extra care hours; Community Supported Living numbers doubled
findings.quote: Services across adult social care reported an overspend of £5.450m, driven by several key pressures... During the year, 126 additional people entered direct payment arrangements and a further 7,158 hours of extra care were delivered.

findings.headline: Council used 100% of contingency budget to manage 2025/26 pressures, leaving no 2026/27 buffer
findings.detail: The council's £5.739m contingency funding was fully deployed to mitigate directorate overspends, with service-level cost pressures of £7.442m offset only by underspends in other budgets of £7.027m. Using all available contingency to balance the ordinary operating budget leaves no buffer for unexpected issues in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Zero contingency remaining signals underlying structural overspends that cannot be absorbed in future years and may require service reductions, reserve drawdown, or budget cuts.
findings.figures: £5.739m contingency used from £5.738m available; service overspends £7.442m offset by £7.027m underspends
findings.quote: Contingency funding played a key role in managing these pressures, with £5.739m of contingency mitigating directorate overspends.

findings.headline: Home to School Transport for SEND pupils surged 8.3%, driving £2.835m overspend
findings.detail: Transport Services overspent by £2.835m on Home to School Transport. SEND passenger numbers rose 8.3% in-year, far exceeding the MTFP assumption of 1.5% overall pupil growth. Actual pupil demand increased 3.9% (720 pupils), with SEND growth driven by increased complexity requiring specialist and single-occupancy journeys.
findings.matters: SEND transport costs are statutory and growing faster than expected due to increased complexity. This suggests ongoing structural pressure that will persist in future budgets.
findings.figures: £2.835m overspend; SEND passenger growth 8.3% vs 1.5% assumed overall; actual pupil growth 3.9% (720 pupils)
findings.quote: Transport Services reported a £2.835m overspend in 2025/26, driven predominantly by pressures within Home to School Transport where demand has grown significantly above assumptions, particularly for pupils with SEND. The MTFP assumed growth of 1.5% in pupil numbers (from 18,689 to 18,969); however, demand increased by 3.9% in-year (c. 720 pupils), with SEND passenger numbers rising by 8.3%

findings.headline: Adult social care equipment provider entered receivership mid-year, creating supply chain risk
findings.detail: Nottingham Rehab Limited (NRS Healthcare), the commissioned provider for the Lincolnshire Community Equipment Service, entered receivership during the year. The council implemented contingency arrangements and incurred £1.287m in additional mobilisation costs to maintain service delivery without interruption.
findings.matters: Provider insolvency in critical care services signals vulnerability in the care market and may indicate other commissioned services face similar pressures, creating unbudgeted costs and service continuity risks.
findings.figures: £1.287m additional mobilisation costs
findings.quote: Nottingham Rehab Limited (NRS Healthcare), the Council's commissioned provider for the Lincolnshire Community Equipment Service, entered receivership, creating a significant risk to the continuity of essential support for vulnerable residents. The Council acted swiftly, working with partners to implement contingency arrangements and maintain service delivery without interruption. These necessary actions resulted in additional mobilisation costs, contributing £1.287m to the overall overspend.

findings.headline: Children's residential placements 73% above budget (85 actual vs 49), driving £8.8m overspend
findings.detail: Children's Social Care had 799 children in care against a budget of 738. Specialist independent placements overspent by £8.824m (54.8% of budget), with residential care placements at 85 against a budget of 49. The overspend was driven by higher numbers and increasing complexity and cost of placements.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in statutory services driven by 73% higher demand than budgeted indicates ongoing structural pressures unlikely to be resolved through service transformation.
findings.figures: 85 residential placements actual vs 49 budgeted; £8.824m overspend; 799 children in care vs 738 budgeted
findings.quote: The most significant pressure relates to specialist independent placements, overspending by £8.824m (54.8%), driven by: • Higher numbers in residential care with 85 placements compared to a budget of 49

findings.headline: High Needs Block has a structural deficit of £25.005m extending beyond 2025/26
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant overspent by £13.406m in 2025/26, driven by the High Needs block. Excluding school balances, this reflects a structural deficit of £25.005m carried forward. Government will support around 90% of deficits to 31 March 2026 through grant funding, but the council must manage the remaining residual risk through future financial planning.
findings.matters: A £25m structural deficit signals long-term unfunded liabilities that could affect creditworthiness and force difficult service or reserve decisions.
findings.figures: £13.406m overspend in 2025/26; £25.005m structural deficit; Government supporting ~90% of deficits
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant overspent by £13.406m, driven by continued pressure within the High Needs block. Excluding school balances, this reflects a structural deficit of £25.005m carried forward.

findings.headline: Finance function insourcing from 24-year Serco contract caused ERP processing delays and revealed unquestioned data quality issues.
findings.detail: The council insourced Finance and Payroll/HR from a 24-year Serco outsourcing arrangement, resulting in ERP processing delays. Post-integration analysis found Serco had met contractual KPIs through unsustainable overtime and temporary staffing. A lessons learned exercise identified that Serco had provided inaccurate data that the council did not challenge during transition. The council has proposed service reorganization and recommended data accuracy be incorporated into future contract management reviews.
findings.matters: Major service transitions expose gaps in supplier oversight and data validation controls; unchallenged data quality from external providers undermines financial reporting accuracy and operational decision-making.
findings.figures: 24-year outsourcing contract insourced; ERP processing delays documented upon integration
findings.quote: The lessons learned findings confirmed that inaccurate data had been shared with the Council prior to integration and that this data had not been challenged by the Council.

findings.headline: Council maintains £453.4m borrowings with negative cash position of £108.3m, indicating overdraft reliance that has worsened year-on-year.
findings.detail: Year-end borrowings of £453.4m (down from £462.1m prior year) are complemented by a negative cash position of (£108.3m), indicating overdraft use for daily cashflow. This overdraft has deteriorated from prior year's (£93.2m), showing increased reliance on short-term financing facilities.
findings.matters: High leverage combined with negative cash position and worsening overdraft dependency signals constrained liquidity and financial strain, critical factors in assessing lending risk and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Year-end borrowings £453.4m (prior year £462.1m); cash position (£108.3m) negative (prior year (£93.2m))
findings.quote: Year-end borrowings £453.4m... Year-end cash position (£108.3m)

findings.headline: Council's usable reserves fell £43.5m to £274.7m, with earmarked reserves drawn down £37.1m and further planned use of £7.8m in 2025-26.
findings.detail: Usable reserves decreased £43.5m (13.7%) from £318.2m to £274.7m, primarily through £37.1m reduction in earmarked reserves to £159.3m. The general fund grew to £24.2m (up 47.6%), but overall reserves are declining despite planning. The council maintained its financial volatility reserve at £46.9m. The 2025-26 budget projects an additional £7.8m reserve use, indicating continued drawdown of financial buffers.
findings.matters: Planned but sustained reserve consumption indicates the council is using financial buffers to maintain service delivery, reducing medium-term financial resilience and strategic flexibility.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £274.7m (down from £318.2m); earmarked reserves £159.3m (down £37.1m); 2025-26 budgeted reserve use £7.8m
findings.quote: The Council's usable reserves have fallen by £43.5m (13.7%), this was largely driven by reduction of £37.1m in earmarked reserves.

findings.headline: Internal audit found 12 high-risk control deficiencies in procurement with inconsistent practices and incomplete documentation retention.
findings.detail: Internal audit's review of contracts and exceptions procedures identified 12 high-risk and 9 medium-risk recommendations. Investigation found varying procurement practices, inconsistent documentation retention, contracts not recorded in the central register, and interest declarations missing. External auditors tested five 2024-25 contracts and found no evidence of inappropriate assessment, but remediation is only 53% complete with 47% of actions still in progress.
findings.matters: Procurement control weaknesses risk inappropriate contracting decisions and inadequate governance oversight, affecting the council's ability to demonstrate value for money and proper stewardship of funds.
findings.figures: 12 high-risk recommendations, 9 medium-risk; 53% of remedial actions completed
findings.quote: Further investigation identified that varying practices were being followed within the procurement team and retention of documentation was inconsistent across contracts. This included numerous contracts not being recorded within the contract register and the documentation of interests not being retained.

findings.headline: Late government funding settlement created inherent risk of misinterpretation across the sector
findings.detail: The provisional settlement was published 17 December and final settlement 9 February, leaving a narrow window for councils to model impacts amid significant funding simplification. The document explicitly states: inherent general risk of misinterpretation or misunderstanding of some of the information. However, the council's position was ultimately found to be favourable.
findings.matters: A lender should understand that the council's budget was prepared under time pressure with novel funding structures. While the current position appears sound, the risk of misinterpretation was real. The council's approach appears to have been cautious.
findings.figures: Settlement published 17 December 2025 (provisional) and 9 February 2026 (final)
findings.quote: given the limited time and scale of information to fully work through including some information not yet published, there is an inherent general risk of misinterpretation or misunderstanding of some of the information across the sector

findings.headline: Pay award inflation estimated at £7.3m but actual amount to be determined later
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes an estimate of £7.3m for pay award inflation, but the budget explicitly notes that the actual amount will depend on the 2026 pay award process outcome. This creates a risk of underprovision if the actual award exceeds the estimate.
findings.matters: A significant cost pressure (£7.3m represents material proportion of total pressures) is not yet fixed. Pay awards in recent years have tracked higher than historical norms, creating overspend risk.
findings.figures: £7.3m estimated; actual amount pending 2026 pay award process
findings.quote: This includes an estimate of pay award inflation in 2026/27 of £7.3m, noting that the actual amount will be determined by the 2026 pay award process.

findings.headline: Lincolnshire business rates pooling ends in 2026/27, eliminating source of growth income
findings.detail: The Lincolnshire business rates pool, which has allowed the council to benefit from growth in business rates across the pool, will not operate in 2026/27. This means no pooling gain this year. This is a direct loss of previously available income, though it is part of wider sector business rates reset.
findings.matters: A lender tracking council income stability should note the loss of pooling gains. This reduces the council's ability to capture business rate growth and may affect future budget flexibility.
findings.figures: Pooling gain in 2026/27: £0
findings.quote: The Lincolnshire business rates pool will not operate in 2026/27, and therefore there will be no pooling gain in 2026/27.

findings.headline: Council is deliberately setting council tax £129 per band D below what Government assumes it can afford
findings.detail: The Government's fair funding model assumes a county council tax rate of £1,836.07, but Lincolnshire is setting it at £1,673.01. This £129.13 gap per band D property scales to approximately £32.1m of available revenue the council is choosing not to raise. The gap widens if the council deviates from government assumptions.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand whether revenue is being maximised or whether the council is deliberately constraining its income. This suggests conservative treasury management but also means less headroom if pressures emerge.
findings.figures: £1,836.07 government assumption vs £1,673.01 actual rate; £129.13 gap per band D; approximately £32.1m total shortfall
findings.quote: The maximum rate of council tax that the Council could set in 2026/27 is £1,706.94 (based on a 4.99% increase). The difference of £129.13, scaled up by the taxbase, equates to an approximate shortfall of £32.1m

findings.headline: Fair funding review confirms Lincolnshire has been historically underfunded, but will gradually receive more
findings.detail: The Government's fair funding review shows the council's share of national need is 1.2189%, but its previous funding share was only 1.0796%. If immediately moved to fair funding, the council would receive an additional £50.5m in 2026/27, though a phased approach means gradual improvement over three years. This reveals the council was operating with systematically constrained resources.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's historical budgets were realistic or whether the council was stretched. Underfunding explains why the council may have deferred investment or kept reserves high.
findings.figures: 1.2189% vs 1.0796% need share; £50.5m additional if fully to fair funding in 2026/27; gains phased over £27m average per year
findings.quote: the new system essentially confirms that the Council has been historically underfunded

findings.committee: Greater Lincolnshire Combined County Authority - Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 4.0 Annual Governance Statement - Year Ending March 2026
findings.headline: Budget holder roles and financial controls still to be introduced as organization evolves
findings.detail: Budget holders have not yet been formally identified and assigned. Budget holder controls will be introduced as the organization moves to its new operating structure and staffing complement grows.
findings.matters: Budget holder controls are fundamental to financial management and accountability. Their absence indicates financial controls are still incomplete.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: As the staffing complement grows, budget holders will be identified and systems of control extended.

findings.committee: Greater Lincolnshire Combined County Authority - Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 4.0 Annual Governance Statement - Year Ending March 2026
findings.headline: Core governance documentation and systems still being embedded into 2026/27
findings.detail: The authority explicitly states that supporting processes remain under development and will be completed and embedded during 2026/27. Standard operating procedures documentation has only recently commenced (section 12).
findings.matters: Complete, embedded governance systems are foundational to financial control and regulatory compliance. Their continued development indicates the organization's control architecture is not yet mature.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: Whilst recognising that supporting processes are still being developed and will be completed and embedded during 26/27, we are satisfied that there has been an adequate framework of controls in place over the financial year 2025/26.

findings.committee: Greater Lincolnshire Combined County Authority - Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 4.0 Annual Governance Statement - Year Ending March 2026
findings.headline: No external audit findings yet; first external audit not complete
findings.detail: GLCCA will receive its first external audit on the 25/26 accounts. This statement covers 2025/26 with no independent external audit results to validate the organization's financial statements or value-for-money arrangements.
findings.matters: External audit provides independent assurance of financial controls and value for money. An organization with no external audit findings yet is without this critical independent check.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: GLCCA will have its first external audit on the 25/26 accounts, and any findings will also inform the 26/27 assurance statement.

findings.committee: Greater Lincolnshire Combined County Authority - Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 4.0 Annual Governance Statement - Year Ending March 2026
findings.headline: Internal audit identified one high-risk governance weakness during the year
findings.detail: Internal audit found one area classified as high-risk in governance arrangements during 2025/26. The statement indicates it has been addressed, but the identification itself signals a control gap in the organization's governance framework.
findings.matters: Governance weaknesses, even when remedied, indicate lapses in control that could affect financial stewardship and regulatory compliance.
findings.figures: One high-risk area identified
findings.quote: One area of high risk was identified in governance and have now been addressed.

findings.committee: Greater Lincolnshire Combined County Authority - Audit Committee
findings.paper_title: 4.0 Annual Governance Statement - Year Ending March 2026
findings.headline: Chief Finance Officer role is interim rather than permanent
findings.detail: The Section 73 Officer (Chief Finance Officer), who holds statutory responsibility for financial management, is in an interim position. This is the lead financial officer for a newly established combined authority with no external audit yet completed.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on stable, experienced financial leadership. Interim status in the CFO role raises questions about continuity and permanent capacity in a young organization.
findings.figures: None stated
findings.quote: Report of: Debbie Simpson, Interim Section 73 Officer, GLCCA

findings.headline: Capital expenditure surge in 2025-26 (£33.4m above original plan) then cliff to £110m baseline creates delivery and cash flow risk
findings.detail: Gross capital expenditure in 2025-26 is £269.882m against an original estimate of £236.485m—a £33.4m increase (14.1%). This is followed by drops to £192.465m (2026-27), £107.690m (2027-28), and £110.123m (2028-29). The peak-and-cliff profile creates execution risk in the high year and suggests either scheme slippage is being accelerated or priorities have shifted materially.
findings.matters: Sharp increases followed by sharp drops create cash flow volatility, delivery risk (can schemes actually be delivered at pace?), and refinancing risk. Lenders assess whether a council can deliver on promised capital schemes and whether the cash flow is manageable.

findings.headline: Capital financing requirement revised down 8.2% mid-year, signalling change in capital program or assumptions
findings.detail: The capital financing requirement for 2025-26 is updated from £811.552m (original estimate) to £744.766m, a reduction of £66.786m. This large mid-year revision—while gross capital spending increases by £33.4m—suggests either schemes have been deferred or financing assumptions have changed. The revision is significant enough to flag material changes to the capital plan between budget approval and revised forecast.
findings.matters: A CFR revision of this magnitude indicates either planning changes, scheme deferrals, or new funding sources. If driven by deferrals or scheme cancellations, it may signal financial pressure. Lenders need to understand whether this reflects good news (more grant), bad news (cuts), or timing shifts.
findings.figures: CFR 2025-26 Original £811.552m → Updated £744.766m (8.2% reduction). Gross capital increased £33.4m despite lower CFR

findings.headline: Grant funding drops £102.6m between 2025-26 and 2026-27, forcing a financing cliff
findings.detail: The 2025-26 updated estimate projects grants and contributions of £179.710m, but this drops to £77.109m in 2026-27—a reduction of £102.6m or 57%. Gross capital expenditure also falls in 2026-27 (to £192.465m), but by only £77.4m, meaning the grant cliff is steeper than the capital drop. This forces the council to switch to alternative funding sources (borrowing, reserves) if capital commitments continue.
findings.matters: Sudden grant withdrawals force either capital schemes to slip, borrowing to spike, or reserves to be drawn. Lenders need confidence that grant assumptions are realistic, contracts locked in, and alternative funding is available if grants reprofiled.

findings.headline: Capital borrowing rising to £82.6m (2026/27) and £119.9m average (2028-2035), creating long-term revenue commitments during tight revenue period
findings.detail: The council is planning capital borrowing of £82.6m in 2026/27, up from £55.6m in 2025/26. Over 2028-2035, borrowing averages £119.9m per year. Rising capital commitments create fixed revenue obligations during a period when the revenue side is extremely tight (£280k surplus, structural demand growth, front-loaded savings). The council acknowledges this tradeoff but commits to re-prioritization to keep costs 'manageable.'
findings.matters: A lender would recognize that rising capital borrowing creates fixed long-term revenue commitments precisely when the council has minimal flexibility. This constrains the ability to respond to demand growth or cost pressures in future years.
findings.quote: Capital decisions create long‑term revenue commitments and are therefore integral to medium‑term financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Cost pressures forecast at £82.6m (2026/27) declining to £43.6m by 2029/30—below recent actual levels and carrying risk of underestimation
findings.detail: The MTFP forecasts cost pressures of £82.6m in 2026/27, declining to £43.6m by 2029/30. This is notably lower than actual cost pressures in recent years: £74.1m (2023/24), £67.9m (2024/25), £83.7m (2025/26). The council acknowledges this introduces 'a degree of risk if pressures subsequently materialise at higher levels than planned.' The 2026/27 balance depends entirely on cost pressures not exceeding forecast, but recent volatility suggests they may.
findings.matters: A lender would identify this as a key sensitivity. If cost inflation does not moderate as forecast—recent volatility suggests this is risky—the council's balanced budget quickly becomes a deficit. This tests whether the financial position can survive realistic cost inflation.
findings.quote: Cost pressures forecast in the later years of the financial plan are lower than those assumed in 2026/27 and below the average level experienced in recent years. While these projections reflect the best information currently available, they introduce a degree of risk if pressures subsequently materialise at higher levels than planned.

findings.headline: Structural demand growth in children's services and adult social care identified as 'the single greatest risk' to financial position
findings.detail: The council identifies demand-led statutory services—particularly children's services (rising numbers requiring statutory intervention, especially SEND) and adult social care (ageing demographics, longer life expectancy, complex needs)—as growing faster than funding. These are explicitly characterized as 'structural in nature' and 'cannot be addressed through short-term measures alone.' The council states these pressures represent 'the single greatest risk to the Council's medium term financial position.' The dominance of statutory services 'limits the Council's ability to absorb cost pressures through marginal reductions elsewhere.'
findings.matters: A lender would view this as the underlying structural unsustainability: the fastest-growing parts of the budget are demand-led and largely uncontrollable, while the council has already cut discretionary services heavily. This creates a long-term funding gap that cannot be closed by efficiency alone.
findings.figures: Budget grows from £868.2m (2026/27) to £996.2m (2029/30), a 14.8% increase; cost pressures £82.6m driven primarily by these demand-led services
findings.quote: In children's services, this is reflected in rising numbers of children requiring statutory intervention, including those with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND). In adult social care, ageing demographics, longer life expectancy and increased prevalence of complex needs continue to drive growth in care and support costs.

findings.headline: 2026/27 budget shows only £280k surplus (0.03% of budget) after delivering £35.5m savings, leaving no room for cost pressures to exceed forecast
findings.detail: The council's 2026/27 budget is balanced only through delivery of £35.5m in planned savings. With a budget requirement of £868.2m and funding of £868.5m, the surplus is just £281k—far too small to absorb unexpected cost growth. The council explicitly acknowledges 'the Council's medium‑term forecast position is sensitive to changes in key assumptions' and that it 'has limited capacity to absorb additional, unplanned pressures.' Any failure on the savings programme or cost inflation above the £82.6m forecast would immediately create a deficit.
findings.matters: A lender would assess this as a zero-margin-for-error budget in a council facing structural cost growth. The savings are heavily front-loaded (£35.5m in 2026/27, declining to £4.9m by 2029/30), suggesting easy wins are taken in year one with limited options for further cuts.
findings.figures: Budget requirement £868.2m, funding £868.5m (2026/27); savings £35.5m (2026/27), £15.4m (2027/28), declining to £4.9m (2029/30); cost pressures £82.6m forecast
findings.quote: The MTFP forecasts implies the Council has limited capacity to absorb additional, unplanned pressures.

findings.headline: Capital programme affordability is improving as the council receives a higher funding base from fair funding changes while the programme has not grown overall.
findings.detail: The council reports medium-term funding certainty and is moving to a higher funding base due to fair funding changes. The capital programme has not grown overall, which combined with the additional funding improves the affordability position. The council has also made voluntary revenue provision payments above the statutory minimum requirement, further reducing the capital financing requirement.
findings.matters: A lender assesses capital affordability by comparing capital commitments against available resources. When a council receives more funding while controlling capital growth, it strengthens debt service capacity and financial resilience.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document; the council does not detail the capital programme size or actual funding amounts in this strategic framework.
findings.quote: the Council is moving to a higher funding base as a result of fair funding changes. Set against a capital programme that has not grown overall, this makes the programme even more affordable than it had already assessed to be.

findings.headline: School assets accounting weakness: revenue spend on council-owned schools incorrectly classified as REFCUS instead of capital.
findings.detail: Testing identified that William Stukeley School expenditure was recorded as REFCUS (revenue expenditure funded from capital) when the school is owned by the council and the spend should have been capitalized as a fixed asset. The auditors recommend a full review of all school assets to verify proper classification and completeness of the asset register.
findings.matters: Systematic misclassification of capital vs revenue spend distorts both balance sheet and revenue position; affects comparability of expenditure and masks the true capital program.
findings.figures: £2.13m of capital spend identified in sample testing that should have been capitalized rather than REFCUS
findings.quote: Testing identified that the Council had recognised REFCUS expenditure against the William Stukeley School, however, further investigation identified that this school was under the ownership of the Council and should have been capitalised. Additionally, testing identified that prior to 2024/25 We recommend that management perform a full review of schools to verify that the school assets included within the asset register exist, are complete and accurate.

findings.headline: Procurement process has significant governance weaknesses: inconsistent practices, unrecorded contracts, and missing documentation.
findings.detail: Internal audit rated the contracts and exceptions review as 'limited assurance', raising 12 high-risk and 9 medium-risk recommendations. Field testing confirmed varying practices across the procurement team, inconsistent document retention, numerous contracts not recorded in the contract register, and missing documentation of interest declarations. As of November 2025, 53% of actions had been fully implemented with 47% still work in progress.
findings.matters: Procurement governance weakness creates fraud risk and fails to demonstrate appropriate oversight of spending; lenders assess councils' ability to manage resources effectively and protect against loss.
findings.figures: 12 high-risk and 9 medium-risk internal audit findings; 53% implemented, 47% work in progress as of audit date
findings.quote: Further investigation identified that varying practices were being followed within the procurement team and retention of documentation was inconsistent across contracts. This included numerous contracts not being recorded within the contract register and the documentation of interests not being retained. There is a significant risk that the inconsistency applied in the procurement process may result in inappropriate contracting decisions being made within the organisation.

findings.headline: No enforced segregation of duties over journal entries; Business World system does not enforce posting limits.
findings.detail: The council's general ledger system (Business World) does not enforce segregation of duties controls over journal posting. Posting limits exist in theory but are not enforced within the system. This is a significant fraud risk that means auditors cannot rely on compensating controls.
findings.matters: Segregation of duties is a foundational fraud prevention control; its absence creates material risk of unauthorized, erroneous, or fraudulent journal entries affecting any account balance.
findings.figures: No quantified impact; control deficiency identified through design and implementation testing
findings.quote: As part of our planning risk assessment procedures we identified that the Council does not have enforced segregation of duty controls over the posting of journals, we will therefore not seek to take a controls based approach when designing procedures to provide assurance over this risk.

findings.headline: Investment property controls (£109m) similarly ineffective; council lacks in-house valuation expertise.
findings.detail: The same control deficiency is identified for the £109m investment property portfolio. The auditors report that management review controls remain ineffective and the council lacks in-house expertise, relying on external valuers (Savills) to determine fair values on an annual basis.
findings.matters: Investment properties generate income for the council; mispricing them materially affects both the balance sheet and revenue position, and signals the control environment cannot detect valuation errors.
findings.figures: £109m investment property as at 31 March 2025; prior year £114.2m (decrease of £5.2m)
findings.quote: Auditing standards require us to report that the design and implementation of the management review control relating to this area remains ineffective in line with the ISA definition. The ISAs acknowledge that it is difficult for management to design controls that address subjectivity in a manner that effectively prevents, or detects and corrects, material misstatements. We also identified that the Council lacks a formal control over the valuation of land and buildings to ensure that relevant valuation was appropriate as the Council does not have the relevant in house valuation expertise.

findings.headline: Management review controls over £649m land and buildings valuation are ineffective, auditors formally report.
findings.detail: The auditors explicitly state that the design and implementation of the council's control over land and building valuations remains ineffective. The council lacks in-house valuation expertise and relies entirely on external valuers (Kier). Of the £649m portfolio, 20% was revalued in the year with the rest indexed.
findings.matters: Land and buildings are the council's largest single asset class; an ineffective control over valuation is a governance weakness that allows no preventive or detective mechanism against material misstatement.
findings.figures: £649m land and buildings as at 31 March 2025; 20% revalued in year; prior year £593.6m (increase of £55.4m)
findings.quote: Auditing standards require us to report that the design and implementation of the management review control relating to this area remains ineffective in line with the ISA definition. The ISAs acknowledge that it is difficult for management to design controls that address subjectivity in a manner that effectively prevents, or detects and corrects, material misstatements. We also identified that the Council lacks a formal control over the valuation of land and buildings to ensure that relevant valuation was appropriate as the Council does not have the relevant in house valuation expertise.

findings.headline: £2.1m of uncorrected audit misstatements left in the financial statements without correction.
findings.detail: The auditors identified misstatements totalling £2.1m (7.2% of surplus on provision of services) that the council chose not to correct. These comprise £2.5m of cash classified as short-term investment when it should be cash equivalent (highly liquid 24-hour deposit), and £2.13m of revenue expenditure capitalized as fixed assets when it should be REFCUS. While auditors state these will have no effect on the opinion, they have formally requested correction.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that stated asset values and classifications are accurate; uncorrected misstatements this large signal either weak financial controls or management's acceptance of material inaccuracy in the accounts.
findings.figures: £2.1m uncorrected misstatements (7.2% of surplus); £2.5m cash/investment classification; £2.13m REFCUS/capital misclassification
findings.quote: The aggregated surplus impact of unadjusted audit differences would be £2.1m. In line with ISA 450 we request that you adjust for these items. However, they will have no effect on the opinion in the auditor's report, individually or in aggregate.

findings.headline: Level 3 investment valuations (£755m) still undergoing retrospective audit review
findings.detail: Level 3 pooled investments—the hardest to value assets relying on unobservable inputs—represent £755.39m or 21.8% of the fund's £3.4bn portfolio. The audit lists 'retrospective review of level 3 investments' as an outstanding matter, with work ongoing and 'no issues noted till date', but final audit sign-off is conditional on satisfactory resolution of these matters.
findings.matters: Level 3 valuations are inherently subjective; incomplete retrospective review of such material holdings leaves audit risk unresolved pending final sign-off.
findings.figures: £755.39m at 31 March 2025 (21.8% of portfolio); prior year £699.32m (21.2%)
findings.quote: Our testing is currently on going and no issues have been noted till date. [outstanding]

findings.headline: Manual journal posting has no enforced segregation of duties controls
findings.detail: The Pension Fund lacks formal segregation of duties when posting manual journals directly to the ledger. Management relies on an informal compensating control (a review of journals impacting balance sheet movements), which auditors cannot rely on for audit purposes. The deficiency stems from ERP functionality limitations in the administering authority's system that cannot be resolved without changes at that level.
findings.matters: A finance director needs assurance that internal controls over financial transactions are robust; informal compensating controls create material fraud risk even when no fraud has been detected.
findings.figures: Not quantified; affects journal entry accuracy and completeness across the £3.4bn pension fund
findings.quote: We identified that there are no segregation of duties controls when posting manual journals directly to the ledger. We identified that management have implemented a compensating control to review any manual journals which impact balance sheet movements, however for the purposes of our audit, we are unable to rely on this control as it is informal in nature.
